title: Turning AI character sheets into consistent sprites for The Fog & Flask — gameplay trailer and workflow
author: Grifxxx
selftext:
I’m developing The Fog & Flask, a potion shop game set in a misty swamp. Here is the English gameplay trailer, along with the asset processing behind the customers you see at the counter.



The useful part of the art workflow has been making separate generated sheets obey the same constraints. Our processing script resizes generated art to a defined pixel grid, quantizes the assets to a shared palette and thresholds alpha so the edges are opaque or transparent. The default palette size is 48 colors. A clean pixel grid alone doesn’t solve inconsistent colors across characters, and a shared palette alone doesn’t remove soft edges, so the stages address different problems.



For guests, the pipeline then separates the frames and assembles the body parts for animation. Hand-authored replacements take priority over generated versions: they bypass the resizing and palette conversion, while still getting trimmed and having their alpha cleaned up. That lets individual assets be replaced without regenerating the whole set.



Those are preprocessing steps; there is no generative AI running during gameplay. Some graphics, including store art, and music were made with AI and selected and edited for the game. Localization also used AI assistance. The game is still in development.



A practical limitation is that palette conversion cannot fix a bad pose or mismatched anatomy. The sheet still needs checking before it becomes an animated character. I’m interested in how others handle that transition from a generated sheet to usable frames.
